episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Wild Spaces & Outdoor Life
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Wild Spaces & Outdoor Life.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: How much should neighbours know about each other?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Cariboo Regional District Board meets for first time of new term and DIY poppy workshop in Williams Lake blends art and stories ahead Remembrance Day, plus 12 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: When a long-lead El Niño warning arrives, what can a place actually do with the lead time, and what does a global forecast leave each place to work out alone? Topics include: Forecast uncertainty and planning under probabilistic warnings (WMO vs. U.S. Climate Prediction Center odds), Health early-warning systems and staffing in Nairobi and Ghana, Coastal flooding, King Tides, and sea-level monitoring in California, Post-wildfire landslide and flood risk in the Cariboo and the Pear Lake fire, Institutional roles: who turns forecasts into named, funded local action.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Family Enrichment Centre

discussion.central_question: When a long-lead El Niño warning arrives, what can a place actually do with the lead time, and what does a global forecast leave each place to work out alone?
discussion.riley_position: Lead time is valuable and should be used now: places should start the first concrete steps (protocols, named assets, funded mapping, contracts) before the damage arrives, sizing actions to the forecast range rather than waiting for certainty.
riley_key_evidence: NOAA's Office for Coastal Management recorded all-time high water levels at four California coastal sites in late October, and the gauges caught the event early.
Nairobi's Bramwell Simiyu says drainage was built for a much smaller population and puts a full sewerage and drainage upgrade at up to $192 million.
Provincial preliminary analysis of the Pear Lake wildfire found high landslide, flood, and debris flow risk in parts of the Cariboo, with risk highest in the two years after a fire.
discussion.casey_position: A warning is not a prepared place: global averages and probabilistic forecasts don't tell a town which asset fails, and without named owners, funding, and maintained maps, lead time gets wasted and the warning becomes a press release.
casey_key_evidence: WMO's September update put the chance El Niño persists through February 2027 near 100 percent, but the U.S. Climate Prediction Center gives only roughly 60 percent odds on a record-strength season.
The Los Angeles Times says the ocean rise is now the larger effect than astronomical tides, and the standard tide table doesn't include that component.
Protocols and mapping decay without ongoing staffing and maintenance, and budget lines can be reallocated by a single motion, so accountability needs a named person.
discussion.resolution: They did not fully resolve the debate; Riley argued for funding and naming owners in budget lines while Casey wanted a named person on the map, and both agreed the regional government should own the turning of forecasts into local action with land users brought in early. Casey closed by saying who decides which creek goes first remains open.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: How strong is the El Niño the WMO is warning about, and how confident are forecasters that it will peak as a record?
Findings: The WMO's State of the Climate Update for COP31 (released November 9, 2026) says El Niño has intensified since August and is expected to reach record strength by December, with higher risk of extreme heat, drought and heavy rainfall into 2027. WMO's September update gave a near-100% likelihood that El Niño would persist through February 2027. The Niño 3.4 index rose from about +1.5°C above normal in May–July 2026 to +2.0°C in July. Wikipedia's event summary describes it as already classified as "very strong" and possibly the strongest on record. The US Climate Prediction Center is less absolute. Its November 12 discussion says El Niño "will continue to strengthen before beginning to weaken in early 2027" and gives roughly 60% odds of a record-strength season for both October–December and November–January. So the persistence of the event is near-certain, but the "record" label is a probability, not a settled fact.
Suggested angle: Riley can argue that this is exactly the kind of case where satellite and buoy monitoring, plus seasonal models, give people months of warning, and that the WMO's forecast is a success story for early warning. Casey can push back that the models only give 60% odds on the record, and that a forecast of "record strength" still leaves real uncertainty for the people who must plan around it. Both can agree that the forecast gives little guidance on exactly where or when the damage will land.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Are the California king-tide flooding reports a one-off, or a measured record that is already happening?
Findings: NOAA's Office for Coastal Management reports that from October 24–30, 2026, California coastal sites recorded elevated water levels above Mean Higher High Water. NOAA tide gauges recorded all-time high water levels at four California coastal sites in late October 2026. The drivers were El Niño-fueled Kelvin waves, a perigean spring tide and an ongoing marine heatwave. The New York Times reports that Los Angeles Harbor logged its highest tide ever, and San Francisco its highest October tide. The Los Angeles Times describes the combination as "only moderately high astronomical tides plus extraordinary/record-breaking ocean level increases," with the ocean-level rise, not the tide itself, now the larger effect. Forecasts for the coming king tides (November 24–26, December 23–25, January 21–22) say they could be half a foot to a foot higher than the tide tables, and NOAA predicts 7.02 ft at Port San Luis on December 24, which could top that gauge's record. The Los Angeles Times also reports that flooding is "quickly becoming a fact of life" in some Southern California coastal communities.
Suggested angle: This is a strong test of the "wild spaces" theme. Riley can frame the NOAA gauges as a sign that coastal monitoring works, and that communities can plan around tide tables and real-time readings. Casey can argue that the coast here is being reshaped faster than planning rules can keep up, and that "a fact of life" is what people say when they have stopped expecting relief. The useful question for the debate is whether a record-setting tide is an unusual event to prepare for, or a new baseline for how people live on the shoreline.

roundup.opening_frame: A day of land, water and weather under pressure, with local council business and a Remembrance craft workshop up front and a run of warnings about what lies ahead.

stories.point: The Cariboo Regional District board held its first meeting of the new term on Nov. 13, electing Margo Wagner as chair and Tolin Pare as vice-chair, and heard a call to balance budgets against property taxes.
stories.bridge_to_next: The Waste Wise workshop is partly funded by the Cariboo Regional District and the City of Williams Lake, so the move from the board to Williams Lake is local.

stories.point: A free upcycled poppy workshop in Williams Lake on Nov. 8, run by the Cariboo Chilcotin Conservation Society's Waste Wise program, let residents make poppy pins from donated fabric while sharing wartime stories.
Oregon Representative Maxine Dexter introduced a bill on Nov. 11 to ban new data centres on national forests and Interior-managed public lands, with 13 Democratic cosponsors.
Demand for salmon is booming, but salmon farmers are closing in on their limits, so cheap salmon may be ending.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both stories are about life in the ocean and how people study or farm it.

stories.point: Woods Hole researchers plan a multiyear study of the SS United States, sunk off Florida on Nov. 11 as an artificial reef, with water samples at 132 locations and tracking of metals released as the steel corrodes.
stories.bridge_to_next: Both are researchers counting and tracking wildlife in remote places, one by sampling a wreck and the other by drone.

stories.point: A drone survey found New Zealand's Erect-crested penguins split in fortune: one island group has been stable for 25 years while the other has declined by more than 40 percent over three decades.
A UN Environment Programme report warns that the world is not adapting to climate costs fast enough, and that wealthy countries have paid out only a fraction of their adaptation pledges.
stories.bridge_to_next: The adaptation shortfall leads to a case of climate change already reshaping the land, thawing permafrost in the Mackenzie Valley.

stories.point: Decades-old wildfires may be thawing permafrost from below in the central Mackenzie Valley, setting off a new kind of landslide.

Environmental groups sued the Trump administration over its third Gulf oil and gas lease sale, held in August, covering more than 81.2 million acres of public waters without National Environmental Policy Act review.
Mountain rescue call-outs in the UK keep setting records, and an outdoor journalist looks at the numbers, the changing demographics and the leading causes.

A synthesis study found that carbon released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, and warmer lakes and wetlands could add 0.2 to 0.4 degrees C of warming this century on top of the 2.6 degrees already expected.
An internal federal memo warns that pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada's long-term security and says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs.

Simon Willison had Claude Code build a system that triangulated an intermittent beep to within about 40 cm using ordinary devices, and the culprit was an old carbon monoxide detector with dying batteries.
Screwworm, eliminated from the U.S. in 1966, is back, and the technique that beat it once will not be enough to get rid of it again.
NASA scientists say the rapidly intensifying 2026 El Niño could grow larger than the 1997-98 event.
stories.bridge_to_next: The El Niño outlook leads to extreme weather already hitting B.C., where heavy rain is forecast for the coast.

stories.point: Environment Canada escalated rainfall warnings for southwest B.C., with more than 250 mm forecast for parts of Vancouver Island after storms that killed two people and cut power to nearly 415,000 BC Hydro customers.
Alberta's Bill 42 would set siting and near-zero cooling-water rules for large data centres and require cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well.
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved construction permits on Nov. 9 for four advanced reactors at Dow's Seadrift plant in Texas, though the permits do not commit Dow to build.

roundup.handoff: Forecasts of extreme weather, from El Niño to the storms already hitting B.C., arrive well ahead of the damage, and the question is what a place does with that lead time.

deep_dive.central_question: A strengthening El Niño is forecast to reach record strength by December and to keep disrupting weather into 2027. When a warning arrives months ahead of the damage, what can a place actually do with that lead time, and what does a global forecast leave each place to work out for itself?
deep_dive.riley_holds: A months-long warning is a real asset, and a place that uses it for specific, affordable preparation, such as early-warning systems and drainage work, comes out ahead.
deep_dive.casey_holds: A global forecast is not a local plan, and lead time is wasted where the underlying systems were built for a smaller, safer world and nobody has funded the fix.

beats.claim: The warning is unusually early and unusually loud, so the lead time is real.
beats.evidence: The WMO says El Niño was declared in early June, began strengthening in August and could reach record strength by December, with disruptive heat and rainfall into 2027 (thesouthafrican.com, energylivenews.com). The WHO has classed the expected health effects as an emergency for the first time for an El Niño and published a Grade 3 preparedness plan (Gizmodo).
beats.pushback: Casey: a loud warning is not the same as a prepared place, and the WMO's own wording is about global averages, with temperatures running about 1.47°C above preindustrial levels from January through September (thesouthafrican.com, gizmodo.com).
beats.leads_to_next: If the warning is real, the test is whether the places it names can use it, so the next beat looks at where the forecast meets concrete systems.

beats.claim: What a place can do with the lead time depends on what it built before the warning arrived.
beats.evidence: Nairobi's disaster-management chief Bramwell Simiyu says the drainage system was built for a much smaller population and a full sewerage and drainage upgrade could cost up to $192 million (BBC). Professor Mawuli Dzodzomenyo says Ghana has weak heat surveillance and few response protocols and calls for early-warning systems (Ghanaian Times).
beats.pushback: Riley: the Ghana example points to a cheap first step, since early-warning systems let health services prepare for heat illness before the season arrives, and that needs no new infrastructure.
beats.leads_to_next: Both agree some steps are cheap and some are not, so the next beat asks what happens when the warning meets a coast that is already exposed.

beats.claim: Where the hazard is already building, a seasonal forecast adds to a risk that is visible now.
beats.evidence: Ocean waters off California are at record heights. Waves above 50 feet hit San Mateo County, seawater filled yards in San Diego, and a wave overtopped a berm at Seal Beach, with the King Tides still to come against a strong El Niño. Damage to homes, highways and wastewater plants is expected, and coastal erosion could be considerable (Scientific American).
beats.pushback: Casey: the weekend damage came before the main event, so lead time guarantees nothing when the water is already at the door and the exposed assets are highways and treatment plants.
beats.leads_to_next: If the first hits come before the peak, then a place has to decide which dated, local warnings it will act on, and the Cariboo has just been through that.

beats.claim: A forecast helps a community most when it is read against local ground, with a named condition and a date.
beats.evidence: From the Nov. 13 episode: the provincial preliminary analysis found high risk of landslides, floods and debris flow in parts of the Cariboo after the Pear Lake wildfire, and the Village of Clinton has already issued a flood Evacuation Alert. This week's roundup also covers heavy rain forecasts and landslide-related evacuations in Zeballos on the coast (theglobeandmail.com).
beats.pushback: Riley: the roundup shows the system working, with warnings escalating and a flood watch issued by the River Forecast Centre before the storm, so the useful thing is to attach each warning to a place.
beats.leads_to_next: This brings the question home to what the burned Cariboo ground needs from a warning, and sets up the landing.

set_aside: EU auditors urge faster PFAS controls: a chemicals-regulation story that does not bear on lead time before extreme weather.
Anthropic's trillion-dollar debut: a financial-markets story with no link to the outdoors or to the warning question.
deep_dive.cariboo_beat: Beat 4: it brings the question to Clinton and the burned country around the Pear Lake wildfire, using the Nov. 13 episode's facts (the provincial analysis and Clinton's flood Evacuation Alert) as the local case of a warning that arrives before the damage. It does not claim El Niño's effect on the Cariboo, since none of today's material says what it will be.
deep_dive.landing: Held open: when a global forecast says a season will be extreme but cannot say what it will do to a particular creek, road or burned slope, who should turn it into a dated local warning, the forecasting agency, the regional government or the people who use the land, and what is lost if each assumes another has.
